title: A Interior for the Language
premise: Lena Yarrow has spent eleven years writing postcards to her mother at an address that burned down, a private ritual that lets her avoid every real conversation in her life. When a demolition crew uncovers a box of undelivered letters behind the wardrobe of the ruined house — letters her mother wrote back, never sent — Lena is forced to read the apology and accusation she always imagined but never received. As the building's demolition date approaches, she must track down the people named in those letters, including a half-sister she never knew existed, and finally speak her goodbye aloud at the site before the walls come down. The novel ends with Lena mailing one last postcard to herself, then burning it unopened: grief answered, not erased.
about_author: Wendell Reyes is the pen name of a former postal clerk who spent nine years sorting dead letters in a coastal city. Their fiction explores what people say when they believe no one will ever answer.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. We meet her writing postcards at a diner counter, deflecting a well-meaning coworker with her practiced smile, and visiting the burned house on Sundays. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as composure; the reader senses the ritual is both wound and shelter.

chapters.title: Postcards to Ash
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, past interwoven. Flashback to the fire and the estrangement that preceded it — the argument about her father that was never finished. She mails card number 4,000. Beat: the ritual's origin revealed as guilt, not love alone.

chapters.title: What the Wardrobe Kept
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. A demolition notice appears on the fence; that night she breaks in for a last look and finds the gap behind the wardrobe — a tin box stuffed with unsent letters addressed to her. Beat: shock curdling into dread; the past has been answering all along.

chapters.title: Letters I Was Never Meant to Read
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. She reads the first three letters in her car through a rainstorm: her mother's voice is funnier, angrier, more alive than memory allowed. Beat: grief complicated by betrayal — these words were withheld from her by someone else's hand.

chapters.title: The Landlord's Nephew
chapters.summary: Alternating POV introducing Theo, the demolition contractor who found the box first and kept it out of the official inventory. He recognizes Lena from her Sunday visits. Beat: wary alliance; two people who both hoard other people's words.

chapters.title: A Name in the Margin
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. A letter mentions 'Ruthie' — a sister born after Lena left home. She begins tracing the name through phone books and parish records. Beat: the ground shifts under her identity; she was not the only daughter.

chapters.title: Justice Is a Small Town with Bad Lighting
chapters.summary: Lena travels to the mother's hometown. She confronts the aunt who helped hide the letters, demanding answers and getting evasions. Beat: anger as engine; Lena discovers the family practiced silence like a trade.

chapters.title: Ruthie Answers the Door
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Ruthie, twenty-six, guarded, works nights at a care home. She knows exactly who Lena is and slams the door. Beat: rejection that mirrors Lena's own deflections; recognition across the threshold anyway.

chapters.title: The Care Home at 3 A.M.
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie reads one of the letters Lena leaves in her locker and weeps where no one can see. She decides, coldly, to test this stranger before trusting her. Beat: grief metabolized into caution; hope handled like something breakable.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Burned House
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo confesses he delayed the demolition permit illegally to give Lena time — and that his own brother died in that fire. Beat: his motive exposed; the box binds three strangers into a reluctant jury.

chapters.title: The Letter That Names a Crime
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. The final letter accuses the uncle — now a respected local judge — of setting the fire to collect insurance, and of intercepting the mail ever since. Beat: the stakes turn legal and mortal; justice outside the law becomes literal.

chapters.title: Everyone Who Benefited
chapters.summary: Lena and Ruthie, working together for the first time, map who gained from the fire: the uncle, the aunt, the silence itself. Beat: sisterhood forged through detective work; dark humor as armor.

chapters.title: The Judge Invites Them to Dinner
chapters.summary: The uncle, warned by the aunt, hosts a chillingly courteous dinner, offering money and a family narrative in exchange for the letters. Beat: menace wrapped in linen napkins; Lena almost takes the deal.

chapters.title: What Survival Cost Her Mother
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, long flashback chapter. The mother's letters reveal the full years: poverty, the fire's aftermath, writing to a daughter she believed had chosen the uncle's side. Beat: compassion replaces blame; Lena understands the smile she inherited.

chapters.title: Ruthie's Condition
chapters.summary: Ruthie's POV. Ruthie agrees to go public only if Lena admits, on record, why she really stopped writing home for those first years. Beat: the confrontation Lena has dodged for eleven years; truth as toll.

chapters.title: Confession on a Bus Bench
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. She tells Ruthie everything — that she saw the uncle with gasoline cans and said nothing, believing her mother chose him over her. Beat: rock bottom; shame spoken aloud loses its grip slightly.

chapters.title: The Demolition Date Moves Up
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The uncle forces the permit through early; they have four days. Theo risks his license to stall the crew. Beat: clock tightening; small acts of sabotage as loyalty.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud at the Fence Line
chapters.summary: Lena, Ruthie, and Theo hold an unofficial hearing outside the house, reading the letters to gathered neighbors while the judge watches from his car. Beat: communal witness; justice as testimony rather than verdict.

chapters.title: The Uncle Breaks
chapters.summary: Climax. Confronted publicly and privately with the last letter, the uncle confesses to the aunt first, then, recorded by Theo's phone, half-confesses to them. Beat: catharsis without triumph; the law may fail them still, but the record exists.

chapters.title: Goodbye, Out Loud
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. On the final morning, inside the gutted house, Lena speaks her goodbye to the empty room where her mother wrote — no paper between them. Ruthie stands beside her. Beat: the ritual completed and released; tears without collapse.

chapters.title: The Walls Come Down
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The demolition proceeds; neighbors watch; the recording goes to a journalist. Theo returns the box to the sisters. Beat: aftermath as shared breath; the house ends so the family can begin.

chapters.title: One Last Postcard
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, epilogue. Months later, Lena writes a postcard to her new address, mails it, receives it, and burns it unread on the beach with Ruthie watching. Beat: quiet resolution; language returned to the living.
